contents.title: Contents
section.whenYouCan.heading: When you can claim compensation
section.whenYouCan.p1: Compensation is money paid to make up for loss, damage or injury caused by a crime. It's a court-ordered payment.
section.whenYouCan.p2: You may be able to claim compensation or apply for benefit payments if you've been affected by a crime.
section.whenYouCan.list: are a victim of a crime
are a close relative of someone who has died because of a crime
witnessed a serious crime, were involved or seriously injured
section.criminalOrders.heading: Criminal compensation orders
section.criminalOrders.p1: If someone is convicted of a crime, the court can order them to pay you compensation. Depending on the circumstances of the case, this could be for:
section.criminalOrders.list1: losses from theft or damage to property
loss, damage, or injury caused by a stolen vehicle
section.criminalOrders.p2: There's no limit on the amount of compensation that can be given under a criminal order. The amount will depend on what the court considers appropriate after looking at the case.
section.criminalOrders.p3: They will consider what's fair, and any evidence and issues raised by:
section.criminalOrders.list2: the person convicted of the crime – for example, how much they can afford to pay without getting into unmanageable debt
the prosecutor – for example, how much compensation you're hoping for
section.criminalInjuries.heading: Criminal injuries compensation scheme
section.criminalInjuries.p1: You might be able to claim compensation if you were the victim of a violent crime. This includes if:
section.criminalInjuries.list: you were physically or mentally injured
you were the victim of sexual assault
you saw the crime happen to a loved one (or were there immediately afterwards)
you paid for the funeral of a person who died
section.criminalInjuries.p2: You usually have to claim within 2 years of the crime. The crime must be reported to the police before you apply.
section.criminalInjuries.linkText: Claim compensation if you were the victim of a violent crime (opens in a new tab)
section.civil.heading: Civil compensation
section.civil.p1: You can make a claim through a civil court. A civil court deals with non-criminal, private cases between people or companies.
section.civil.p2: For example, you could claim compensation for personal injury, assault or damage to property.
section.civil.p3: You should get legal advice first, as the process can be difficult and expensive.
section.benefits.heading: Claiming benefits
section.benefits.p1: Depending on your circumstances, there might be benefits you can claim.
section.benefits.p2.linkText: benefits and financial support when someone dies (opens in new tab)
section.benefits.p3.before: If you're refused a benefit and you disagree, you can
section.benefits.p3.linkText: appeal a benefits decision (opens in new tab)
section.insurance.heading: Insurance for your property
section.insurance.p1: You can check your home or car insurance policy to see if it covers the crime you experienced, for example theft or vandalism to your property.
section.insurance.p2: If someone committed a crime to your property and you have their details, you might be able to make a claim against their insurance policy.
section.insurance.p3.before: If an insurance company refuses a claim and you disagree, you can complain to the
section.insurance.p3.linkText: Financial Ombudsman Service (opens in new tab)
section.employment.heading: Employment insurance
section.employment.p1: If the crime involved an injury or death that happened at your work, you might be able to make an insurance claim against your employer.
section.employment.p2: Most employers are legally required to have insurance to cover employees for injury, illness, or death that occurs as a result of their work.
section.employment.p3: You would need to document the incident and instruct a solicitor who sends a "letter of claim" to your employer or their insurer.
